title: Court Case Preparation — August 10, 2026
description: Complete study module for your 74th District Court hearing

sections.title: Your Case Overview
sections.content: Case: 74th District Court, Bay City. Case Number: 26-4144-SC. Date: Monday, August 10, 2026, 9:30 AM. Magistrate: Perry. Plaintiff: Jolene D. Wilcox. Incident: June 7, 2026 vehicle collision. Amount claimed: $5,664.68 (vehicle damage, towing, storage). Key fact: The mini-tort cap limits recovery to $3,000 for vehicle damage. The claim exceeds this cap. Towing and storage are likely NOT covered by the mini-tort (which covers damage to the vehicle only). Even if included, total mini-tort recovery is still capped at $3,000. The mini-tort is the EXCLUSIVE remedy for vehicle damage — the plaintiff cannot pursue a separate 'general tort' for the car. Both parties show GEICO on the UD-10 crash report, but the plaintiff has not provided proof of active insurance with her filing.

sections.title: Your Rights as Defendant
sections.content: Right to present evidence (bring all documents, photos, witnesses). Right to cross-examine witnesses (within informal hearing format). Right to request adjournment (NOT guaranteed — judge decides). NO ATTORNEY MAY APPEAR in small claims (MCL 600.8408(1)) — if you want a lawyer, case must be removed to general civil division before trial. Right to file counterclaim (must have independent legal basis and provable damages). Right to appeal magistrate decision to district judge within 7 days (MCL 600.8427). Right to request the plaintiff produce proof of insurance. The UD-10 crash report is NOT conclusive proof of active coverage — officers only record what's on the card, they don't verify with the insurance company. Direct verification (declarations page, letter of coverage, claim check) is required to prove the policy was active on the date of the accident. Because the mini-tort is the EXCLUSIVE remedy for vehicle damage (MCL 500.3135(3)), the plaintiff cannot 'elect' a higher general-tort claim for the car. You can raise this: the cap and the exclusive-remedy rule govern.

sections.title: Michigan Law & the Mini-Tort
sections.content: SMALL CLAIMS: Jurisdiction MCL 600.8401. Jurisdictional ceiling: $7,000 since January 1, 2024 (MCL 600.8401(e)). Statute of limitations: 3 years for tort claims (MCL 600.5805(2)). Burden of proof: preponderance of the evidence. MINI-TORT (MCL 500.3135): Capped at $3,000 for accidents after July 1, 2020 (MCL 500.3135(3)(e)). This is an AMOUNT DEFENSE — it limits recovery, not a dismissal. THE MINI-TORT IS EXCLUSIVE (VERIFIED): MCL 500.3135(3) abolishes tort liability for vehicle damage where the required security (MCL 500.3101(1)) was in effect. The only surviving vehicle-damage remedy is the mini-tort exception (3)(e). The plaintiff CANNOT elect a general tort for the car. NO $5,000 GENERAL-TORT CEILING (VERIFIED): $5,000 was the small-claims ceiling ONLY 9/1/2012–12/31/2014. Current small-claims ceiling is $7,000 (MCL 600.8401(e)). For vehicle damage, the operative limit is the $3,000 mini-tort cap. $3,000 CAP APPLIES REGARDLESS OF CLAIM AMOUNT (VERIFIED): it is an amount/damages cap, not a jurisdictional dismissal bar. The $5,664.68 claim proceeds (under the $7,000 court ceiling) but vehicle-damage recovery is capped at $3,000. TOWING/STORAGE (INTERPRETATION): likely NOT within 'damages ... to a motor vehicle'; even if included, total is still capped at $3,000. CORRECT CITATION (VERIFIED): property damage / 'property protection' (PPI) = MCL 500.3121. MCL 500.3105 is PIP (bodily injury), NOT property — do not cite 3105 for property. PLAINTIFF MUST PROVE: (1) she was 50% or less at fault, (2) her vehicle had no-fault insurance on June 7, 2026, (3) the damages were not covered by her own insurance. If she cannot prove active insurance, the mini-tort claim may be barred under MCL 500.3135(4)(e). The UD-10 crash report shows GEICO for both parties, but it is police-reported information — the plaintiff should produce proof of coverage (declarations page, policy document, or insurance card). The UD-10 is NOT proof of active coverage: a policy could have been canceled before the accident. STRATEGY: State the mini-tort cap ($3,000 max), request direct proof of insurance from GEICO, challenge towing/storage as not covered by the mini-tort, present your own documentation of damages.

sections.title: What to Say & Argument Order
sections.content: SAFE PHRASES: 'I'm here to respond to the claim.' 'The mini-tort cap limits recovery to $3,000 for vehicle damage. The claim exceeds this amount.' 'I applied my brakes at the stop sign.' 'I have documentation of my own damages.' INSURANCE / UD-10 SCRIPT: 'Your Honor, the UD-10 crash report only shows what the officer recorded from the insurance card. It does not verify the policy was active on June 7, 2026. I request that the plaintiff produce direct verification from GEICO — a declarations page, letter of coverage, or claim check.' If she cannot produce direct proof, add: 'Your Honor, if the plaintiff cannot produce direct proof that her policy was active on June 7, 2026, the mini-tort claim should be barred under MCL 500.3135(4)(e).' LEGAL ARGUMENT (add this line): 'Vehicle damage is governed by the exclusive mini-tort remedy, capped at $3,000 (MCL 500.3135). There is no separate general tort the plaintiff can pursue for the car, and towing/storage are not vehicle damage covered by the mini-tort.' ORDER OF ARGUMENTS — PSYCHOLOGY OF PERSUASION: (1) CONCEDE WHAT YOU CAN'T WIN: 'I don't deny the collision happened, and I don't deny Ms. Wilcox's car was damaged.' This buys maximum credibility. (2) PRESENT YOUR ACCOUNT: 'I applied my brakes at the stop sign. The absence of skid marks suggests the brakes may not have responded as expected. The police report captures one perspective — I'd like to present my account.' (3) CITE THE LAW: 'Under MCL 500.3135, any recovery for vehicle damage is capped at $3,000, reduced by comparative fault, and only to the extent not covered by insurance. The claim exceeds this cap.' (4) REQUEST SPECIFIC RELIEF: 'I ask that any recovery be reduced by the plaintiff's share of fault, capped at the $3,000 statutory limit, and only to the extent the damages are not covered by insurance.' Plant seeds of doubt through QUESTIONS, not accusations: 'I ask the court to weigh...' not 'She's wrong.'

sections.title: How to Open
sections.content: YOUR OPENING — EXACT SCRIPT: 'Good morning, Your Honor. I'm Sophia Saitta, the defendant in this matter. I'm here to respond to the claim, and I'd like to give my account of what happened.' THAT'S IT. Name + purpose + readiness. Do NOT make a speech about yourself. Do NOT say what you do for a living unless it's relevant. The magistrate has 20 cases today. Competence and calm win, not credentials. If you want to mention your work, use it as a grounding line: 'I run a technology company, Your Honor, so I'm used to being organized — I want to assure you I've come prepared to be straightforward about what happened.'

sections.title: Your Closing Statement
sections.content: YOUR CLOSING — MEMORIZE THIS: 'Your Honor, I came here to be straightforward. I don't deny the collision happened, and I don't deny Ms. Wilcox's car was damaged. But I ask that you weigh the ambiguity in the physical scene against the report, that any recovery reflect that this was not solely my responsibility, that it be capped at the $3,000 statutory limit for vehicle damage, and that the towing and storage be supported by receipts and only to the extent not covered by insurance. Whatever you decide, I appreciate your time and consideration.' WHY THIS WORKS: It concedes what you can't win (buys credibility), restates your three winning points (comparative fault, cap, documented damages), and ends with grace and respect. End with thanks, not threats.

sections.title: What NOT to Say / Forbidden Moves
sections.content: WHAT NOT TO SAY — DO NOT: Admit fault (the police report shows your vehicle failed to stop at a stop sign). Rely on the '$3,000 means I can't be sued' theory — this is WRONG. The $3,000 is a mini-tort cap on recovery, NOT a jurisdictional ceiling. Make emotional statements. Discuss legal theories you can't support. Say anything about insurance without careful thought. Argue the plaintiff was uninsured — only argue she hasn't proven her policy was active. The UD-10 shows GEICO was listed, but that's not the same as proof the policy was in force. FORBIDDEN MOVES — READ BEFORE ENTERING: ❌ Interrupting anyone. ❌ Arguing with the magistrate. ❌ Admitting fault ('I ran the sign'). ❌ 'The brakes failed' — sounds like a vehicle maintenance admission. ❌ 'She didn't brake' — speculation without evidence. ❌ 'She's lying' — inflammatory and unprofessional. ❌ 'She has no insurance' — UD-10 shows GEICO; say 'hasn't proven her policy was active.' ❌ 'I owe nothing' — loses credibility; you're conceding the collision happened. ❌ Reacting visibly to plaintiff's testimony. ❌ Rambling — you have ~3-5 minutes of speaking time. Be brief, be specific, be done. ADDITIONAL WRONG ARGUMENTS: ❌ 'There's a $5,000 ceiling so I only owe $5,000' — WRONG; no such $5,000 general-tort ceiling exists (mini-tort $3,000 is the cap). ❌ 'She can pursue a general tort instead' — WRONG; the mini-tort is the exclusive remedy for vehicle damage.

sections.title: Courtroom Procedure
sections.content: IMPORTANT: Both in-person AND Zoom are checked on your packet. Call the court (989-895-4232 or 989-895-4203) to CONFIRM before Monday. If in-person: arrive by 9:00 AM (30 minutes early) and check in with the clerk. If Zoom: Meeting ID 946-661-3202, do NOT join early or late. SMALL CLAIMS PROCEDURE — WHAT HAPPENS WHEN: (1) Check-in: arrive 30 minutes early, check in at clerk's window. Phone off, notes ready. (2) Call & Identification: Magistrate calls the case number, both parties state names, both sworn in. Stand when speaking (if in-person). (3) Plaintiff's Case: Plaintiff speaks FIRST for 5-8 minutes. She presents documents, calls witnesses. DO NOT INTERRUPT. Take notes. (4) Your Case: Magistrate turns to you. Give your planned response. You may ask the plaintiff questions. (5) Magistrate Questions: Magistrate probes both sides. Answer honestly, don't argue. (6) Closing: Short statements from both sides. Ask: 'Your Honor, may I make a brief closing statement?' (7) Decision: Magistrate rules immediately or takes under advisement (decision mailed). Either way, write down the result. 7-day appeal window. TAKE NOTES — there is NO court reporter and NO verbatim record (MCL 600.8411(2)). Your notes are the only record of what happened. EXPECT 20-30 MINUTES TOTAL.

sections.title: Risk Assessment
sections.content: CRITICAL: The police report (UD-10, Officer Jacob Kirsch) states Unit 1 (your vehicle) failed to stop at the stop sign and caused the collision. This is documented evidence. The claim amount ($5,664.68) exceeds the mini-tort cap ($3,000). A finding against you on the mini-tort limits your exposure to $3,000 for vehicle damage — this cap applies regardless of the claim amount. Towing/storage are likely NOT covered by the mini-tort; at most they are included within the $3,000 cap, not added on top. Because the mini-tort is the exclusive remedy, the plaintiff cannot turn to a separate general tort for the car (MCL 500.3135(3)). Be prepared to respond to the stop-sign evidence without admitting fault.

sections.title: Documents to Bring
sections.content: CRITICAL DOCUMENTS FOR COURT: (1) The 11-page filing/packet from plaintiff. (2) Case number: 26-4144-SC (write on sticky note). (3) Your insurance documents/policy. (4) Photos of vehicle damage (both cars if available). (5) Police/citation records from June 7 incident. (6) Your own repair estimates or receipts. (7) Any correspondence with insurance companies. (8) Notepad and pen — THERE IS NO COURT REPORTER. (9) This study guide — print the Quick Reference card. (10) A list of what direct verification from GEICO looks like (declarations page, letter of coverage, claim check) so you can recognize it. (11) Arrive with an organized folder, not loose papers.

sections.title: Staying Calm Under Pressure
sections.content: NAVY SEAL CALM — HOW TO STAY CENTERED: (1) Box Breathing: In 4 counts, hold 4, out 4, hold 4. Repeat 5 times before entering. (2) Posture: Feet flat, back straight, hands still. Open, grounded posture projects confidence. Do NOT cross arms or fidget. (3) Eye Contact: Look at the magistrate when speaking and when they speak. Steady, not a stare-down. Strongest credibility signal. (4) Slow Down: Before answering, take one small breath and a half-second pause. You are never in a hurry. (5) Notepad: Write things down. It anchors you. (6) Mantra: 'I'm the calmest, most reasonable adult here.' (7) Reframe: This is capped at $3,000 — not life or death. You cannot lose your freedom. The downside is bounded. If you blank: 'Your Honor, I'd like a moment to check my notes.'

sections.title: Psychology of the Courtroom
sections.content: THE PSYCHOLOGY OF WINNING — FROM PSYCHE (Psychological Artisan): THE MAGISTRATE'S TRIFECTA: (1) Credibility — strategic concession + no over-claiming + calm correction + steady eyes. (2) Preparation — arrive early, organized documents, cite statute once precisely, take notes, have police report ready to hand up. (3) Reasonableness — frame every doubt as evidence, not accusation; concede the accident; treat plaintiff with courtesy; yield to court's authority. NEUTRALIZE THE VICTIM SCHEMA: You cannot beat 'I was hit' head-on — she IS the injured party. Do not try to make her the villain. Instead, win the AMOUNT and COMPARATIVE FAULT. Redirect from 'who's at fault' to 'what's fair and provable.' The victim schema wins sympathy; the cap and evidence win the number. BUILD YOUR 'HONEST, REASONABLE' SCHEMA: Concede something real early ('I don't dispute the accident happened') — the magistrate's brain files you as honest. Every subsequent denial is assimilated into that honest frame. The gratitude frame (thanking the court) activates reciprocity — the magistrate unconsciously wants to give the courteous party the benefit of the doubt. UNCONSCIOUS TRUST LEVERS (ranked): (1) Calm — edges out everything; a calm party is presumed honest. (2) Strategic concession — honesty signal. (3) Specificity — dates, dollar figures, details you recall. Vague people are suspicious; specific people are believed. (4) No weasel words — no 'maybe,' 'I guess,' 'possibly not.' State what you know firmly; mark what you don't know honestly. (5) Courtesy to the plaintiff — treated well, she does the work of making you look decent. (6) Respect for the bench — yield to magistrate's control, never argue. THE ONE MOVE THAT WINS: Make the magistrate's job easy. Give her a clean story, a clean number, and a reason to side with you she can defend. When a magistrate can rule for you AND point to the statute, she rules for you. Your job is to hand her that statute and that number without making it feel like a fight.

quiz.question: What does MCL 500.3135(3) do?
options: Abolishes tort liability for vehicle damage
quiz.explanation: MCL 500.3135(3) abolishes general tort liability for vehicle damage where required security was in effect — the mini-tort is the EXCLUSIVE remedy.

quiz.question: What is the mini-tort cap?
quiz.explanation: The mini-tort cap is $3,000 for accidents after July 1, 2020 (MCL 500.3135(3)(e)).

quiz.question: When did the $3,000 cap take effect?

quiz.question: What does MCL 500.3101(1) require?
quiz.explanation: MCL 500.3101(1) requires an owner to maintain no-fault security. This is the 'required security' that triggers the mini-tort as the exclusive remedy.

quiz.question: What is MCL 500.3121?
quiz.explanation: MCL 500.3121 is property protection insurance (PPI). It's property damage — NOT 500.3105 which is PIP/bodily injury. Do not cite 3105 for property.

quiz.question: What is the statute of limitations?

quiz.question: How long is the hearing?
quiz.explanation: Expect the whole hearing to last roughly 20-30 minutes total.

quiz.question: Who speaks first?
quiz.explanation: The plaintiff speaks first for 5-8 minutes, presenting documents and witnesses. Listen and take notes; don't interrupt.

quiz.question: How long does each party speak?
quiz.explanation: Each party gets about 5-8 minutes to present their case. Be brief, be specific, be done.

quiz.question: What should you do while the plaintiff speaks?
quiz.explanation: There is no court reporter, so take detailed notes. Do NOT interrupt the plaintiff while she presents her case.

quiz.question: Can you ask the plaintiff questions?
quiz.explanation: Yes — when it's your turn, you may ask the plaintiff questions. Plant seeds of doubt through questions, not accusations.

quiz.question: What should you say when asked if you're ready?
quiz.explanation: Answer with confidence: 'Yes, Your Honor.' Avoid weasel words like 'I guess' — they undermine credibility.

quiz.question: What happens if the magistrate needs more time?
quiz.explanation: The magistrate either rules immediately or takes the case under advisement, mailing the decision later. Either way, write down the result.

quiz.question: How do you ask for a closing statement?
options: "Your Honor, may I make a brief closing statement?"
Just keep talking past your time
quiz.explanation: Ask politely: 'Your Honor, may I make a brief closing statement?' — courtesy to the bench counts.

quiz.question: What is PSYCHE's trifecta?
quiz.explanation: The magistrate's trifecta: Credibility (strategic concession + calm), Preparation (organized documents + precise citations), Reasonableness (frame doubt as evidence, not accusation).

quiz.question: What is the #1 unconscious trust lever?
quiz.explanation: Calm edges out everything — a calm party is presumed honest. It's the #1 unconscious trust lever.

quiz.question: What should you concede early?
options: That the full amount is owed
That you ran the stop sign
quiz.explanation: Concede the collision happened ('I don't deny the accident occurred') — never concede fault or the full amount.

quiz.question: What is the psychology of strategic concession?
quiz.explanation: Strategic concession triggers the consistency principle: concede something real and the magistrate's brain files you as honest.

quiz.question: What should you never do during the plaintiff's testimony?
quiz.explanation: Never react visibly to the plaintiff's testimony — no eye-rolling, sighing, or head-shaking. Stay calm and composed.

quiz.question: What is the forbidden move regarding the magistrate?
quiz.explanation: Never argue with the magistrate. Yield to the bench's control — respect the court's authority.

quiz.question: What should you say if you blank on a legal point?
options: "Your Honor, I'd like a moment to check my notes"
quiz.explanation: If you blank, say: 'Your Honor, I'd like a moment to check my notes.' It's composed and takes the pressure off.

quiz.question: What is the mantra for staying calm?
options: "I have to win no matter what"
"I'm the calmest, most reasonable adult here"
quiz.explanation: Repeat the mantra: 'I'm the calmest, most reasonable adult here.' Reframe: the downside is bounded at $3,000.

quiz.question: What does the UD-10 show for both parties?
quiz.explanation: The UD-10 crash report lists GEICO for both parties — but that is not proof the policy was active.

quiz.question: Why is the UD-10 not proof of active coverage?
options: Officer only records what's on the card
quiz.explanation: Police only record what's on the insurance card. They don't call the insurer to verify the policy was active on the date of the accident.

quiz.question: What is direct verification?
options: Declarations page, letter of coverage, claim check
quiz.explanation: Direct verification means a declarations page, letter of coverage, or claim check from GEICO — not the police report.

quiz.question: What should you ask the plaintiff about insurance?
quiz.explanation: Ask: 'Can you produce direct verification?' — a declarations page, letter of coverage, or claim check showing active coverage on June 7, 2026.

quiz.question: What happens if plaintiff can't prove insurance?
quiz.explanation: If the plaintiff cannot prove active insurance, the mini-tort claim may be barred under MCL 500.3135(4)(e).

quiz.question: What is MCL 500.3135(4)(e)?
quiz.explanation: MCL 500.3135(4)(e) bars damages if the vehicle lacked the required security at the time of the accident — the no-security bar.

quiz.question: Can you say 'she was uninsured'?
options: No, say "hasn't proven her policy was active"
quiz.explanation: Never assert 'she was uninsured.' The UD-10 shows GEICO. Say she 'hasn't proven her policy was active.' This is the safe, accurate framing.

quiz.question: What is the safest way to raise insurance?
options: Ask for direct verification, don't assert
quiz.explanation: Raise insurance by asking for direct verification — don't assert she lacks coverage. Assertions backfire; a request for proof is credible.
